newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian coal exports to rise, prices fall.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian coal exports to rise, prices fall.

text.p: Australia's coal export earnings are forecast to rise 3.4 percent in 1997/98 as higher volumes compensate for a fall in prices, said the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE).
In its March quarter Commodities bulletin, ABARE forecast export earnings of A$8.19 billion in the year to June 30, 1998 from an estimated A$7.92 billion in 1996/97.

Australian production was forecast to rise 5.4 percent in 1997/98 to 214 million tonnes from an expected 203 million this year, although ABARE said there was a risk reduced profitability in the industry would cut into that.

"Given a forecast price fall of nearly 3.5 percent for Australian export coal in 1996/97 and a further 3.0 percent forecast fall in 1997/98 it is expected that the profitability of the industry, particularly that of some new projects, may be reduced," ABARE said.
"As a consequence, their commissioning may be postponed until prices are more favourable," the agency said.

Despite the fall in prices, Australian coal exports were forecast to rise seven percent to 156 million tonnes in 1997/98 so delivering the expected rise in total export earnings. Coal exports were seen up 5.4 percent in 96/97 to 146 million tonnes.
ABARE noted Australian thermal coal producers had agreed to a US$2.65 a tonne cut in prices from Japanese buyers in the 1997/98 Japanese fiscal year to US$40.30 a tonne.
"The fall reflects excess market market supply, most evident in spot purchases by Asian coal users in 1996 at significant discounts to benchmark prices," ABARE said.
The agency said semi-soft coking coal prices fell around A$2.00 a tonne in negotiations with Japanese steel mills, while hard coking coal prices dipped around A$0.20 a tonne.
World demand for thermal coal was expected to grow strongly in 1997/89 but should be readily met by increasing supplies.
That in turn was expected to force down world thermal prices, ABARE said.

World thermal coal trade was forecast to increase by four percent in the 1997 calender year, with around 70 percent of this growth in Asia where a number of coal fired power stations should be coming on stream.
An expected recovery in world steel production was expected to lead to an increase in world metallurgical coal demand over the next year, the agency said.

However, growth in coal supply and further increases in the use of lower quality coals in blast furnace steel production, particularly in Japan, were expected to result in the weighted average contract rpice of Australian metallurgical coal falling around US$0.75 to US$48.12 a tonne in 1997/98.
ABARE said it expected Australian producers to increase their share of the Japanese market for hard coking coal, largely at the expense of Canadian producers.
Australia was also expected to increase exports to Taiwan, South Korea and India.
